reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India national programmes
clinicalPearls: A soil-transmitted intestinal nematode acquired when larvae in contaminated soil penetrate skin, endemic in warm, humid parts of India
Uniquely among common helminths it can complete its life cycle within the host (autoinfection), so infection may persist silently for decades
Chronic infection is often mild, with intermittent abdominal symptoms, urticaria, and a characteristic migratory serpiginous rash (larva currens); eosinophilia is a common clue
The feared complication is hyperinfection/disseminated disease, precipitated by immunosuppression, especially corticosteroids and HTLV-1 co-infection
Screening and treating latent infection before starting immunosuppression is a key preventive principle
Disseminated strongyloidiasis often carries Gram-negative bacteraemia or meningitis as larvae transport gut bacteria
A single stool examination is insensitive; serology and repeated or concentrated stool studies improve detection
Antiparasitic therapy with ivermectin is the treatment principle, with prolonged/repeated courses needed in disseminated disease
reference.pathophysiology: Filariform larvae penetrate the skin, migrate through the circulation to the lungs, ascend the airways and are swallowed, maturing into adult worms in the small intestine. Females produce eggs that hatch into rhabditiform larvae; some transform into infective filariform larvae within the gut or perianal skin and reinvade the host, sustaining autoinfection. When host cellular immunity is impaired, this autoinfective cycle accelerates uncontrollably, causing massive larval migration through multiple organs (hyperinfection and dissemination) and carrying enteric bacteria that seed the bloodstream, meninges and other sites.
additionalDifferentials: Peptic ulcer disease or functional dyspepsia
infectionMimics: Other causes of Gram-negative sepsis in the immunosuppressed
additionalInvestigations: Serology for Strongyloides antibodies, which is more sensitive than single stool testing
Repeated stool microscopy with concentration or agar-plate culture to detect larvae
Full blood count looking for eosinophilia (which may be absent in dissemination)
Examination of sputum, duodenal aspirate or other fluids for larvae in suspected hyperinfection
Screening for HTLV-1 and assessment of immune status in severe disease
redFlags: Hyperinfection or dissemination in an immunosuppressed patient, a life-threatening emergency
Gram-negative bacteraemia or meningitis complicating heavy larval migration
Planned corticosteroid or other immunosuppression in someone from an endemic area without prior screening
Rapid respiratory or gastrointestinal deterioration with detectable larvae
reference.prognosis: Chronic uncomplicated infection responds well to antiparasitic therapy and has an excellent outlook, though eradication should be confirmed given the autoinfection risk. Hyperinfection and disseminated disease, by contrast, carry very high mortality despite treatment, particularly when diagnosis is delayed.
pitfalls: Starting corticosteroids or immunosuppression without screening at-risk patients, precipitating fatal hyperinfection
Relying on a single negative stool sample to exclude infection
Assuming eosinophilia will always be present, as it is often absent in dissemination
Failing to give a sufficiently prolonged antiparasitic course in disseminated disease
management: Definitive anthelmintic therapy with ivermectin as first line for chronic infection, with albendazole as an alternative or adjunct
Screen for and treat latent infection before starting immunosuppression, particularly corticosteroids, and in HTLV-1 co-infection
Confirm cure with follow-up serology and stool examination given the risk of persistent autoinfection, repeating or extending treatment as required

Hyperinfection or disseminated disease: prolonged ivermectin continued until larvae are cleared, reduction or withdrawal of immunosuppression, and parenteral or veterinary-formulation ivermectin where enteral absorption is impaired
Treat accompanying Gram-negative bacteraemia or meningitis with broad-spectrum antibiotics alongside organ support in intensive care
Preventive advice on footwear and sanitation in endemic areas and screening of at-risk migrants and transplant or immunosuppression candidates
Involve infectious diseases specialists for severe or disseminated disease
